card.title: Electromotive Force of a Source, Internal Resistance

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A real source has **internal resistance** r. Its **emf** E is the work per unit charge driving charge around the whole circuit (the open-circuit voltage); the **terminal voltage** under current I is $V = E - Ir$ — the internal drop is lost inside. Kirchhoff's laws organise any circuit: **KCL** (ΣI = 0 at a junction — charge conservation) and **KVL** (ΣE = ΣIR round a loop — energy conservation).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - V = E − Ir (discharge); V = E + Ir (charging) - I = E/(R + r) - KCL: ΣI = 0 at a junction; KVL: ΣE = ΣIR in a loop

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: EMF vs Terminal Voltage: EMF $\mathcal{E}$ is the open-circuit terminal voltage ($I=0$). Terminal voltage $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ drops as current increases due to internal resistance.  ·  Internal Resistance Effects: Internal resistance causes voltage drop ($Ir$), power loss ($I^2r$), and heating inside the source. It limits maximum deliverable current and power.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Kirchhoff's voltage law: the algebraic sum of the emfs in a closed loop equals the algebraic sum of the potential drops."

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **EMF ≠ terminal voltage:** V = E − Ir once current flows; they coincide only when I = 0.  ·  **KCL conserves charge; KVL conserves energy** — quote both physics reasons.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Why Batteries Sag Under Load A battery's label promises 1.5 V or 12 V, but the voltage you measure drops when it works hard. The hidden culprit is **internal resistance** — and Kirchhoff's laws are the tools that track every volt and every ampere around a real circuit.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2022, 2024) ### 2.1 EMF and terminal voltage - **EMF (E):** the work done per unit charge by the source in driving charge around the *whole* circuit — the open-circuit terminal voltage. - **Terminal voltage (V):** the actual potential difference across the terminals when current I flows: $$V = E - Ir$$ — the internal drop Ir is "lost" inside the source.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "I = E/(R + r); V = IR = E − Ir — compute both ways as a check."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): E = 9 V, r = 1 Ω, R = 8 Ω. Find I, V and the internal drop.** — I = 1 A; V = 8 V; internal drop = 1 V (dissipated inside the battery).

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: State the conservation principle behind each Kirchhoff law — examiners look for it.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The internal drop Ir is the voltage the circuit never sees.**

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: V = E − Ir; I = E/(R + r); KCL junctions, KVL loops.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Car headlights dim at starting because the starter's huge current makes Ir eat the battery's emf.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Maximum Power Transfer: Maximum power is delivered to load when load resistance equals internal resistance ($R = r$). This is important for matching circuits but not for efficiency (efficiency is only 50% at this point).  ·  Verified PYQs: Kirchhoff + circuit (2022, 2024 — 5m each); terminal voltage (2024, 3m).  ·  Why does a battery feel warm after heavy use?
